newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo prosecutors raid DKB executives' homes - Jiji.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo prosecutors raid DKB executives' homes - Jiji.

text.p: Tokyo prosecutors raided the homes of current and former executives of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd on Wednesday, Jiji news service said.
The move followed similar raids on a number of locations including DKB's headquarters and the homes of several bank officials on Tuesday.
Prosecutors raided about 10 locations on Wednesday in connection with their investigation into a racketeer payoff scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd, it said.
A DKB spokeswoman said the public relations department of the bank had not received any information about the raids.
Jiji said prosecutors were believed to suspect the involvement of DKB executives in questionable loans to a racketeer at the centre of the Nomura scandal.
Japanese media reports have said DKB provided questionable loans to the racketeer, Ryuichi Koike, who was arrested last week.
The bank has repeatedly declined comment on its reported link with Koike.
On Tuesday, officials of the Tokyo Public Prosecutors' Office said they had raided DKB in connection with the alleged violation of the commercial code by Nomura.

Meanwhile, Kyodo news agency said DKB chairman Tadashi Okuda and president Katsuhiko Kondo were expected to resign to take responsibility for DKB's involvement in the scandal. The formal decision will be made at the bank's annual shareholders' meeting in June, it said.
The DKB spokeswoman said no such decision had been made.
Kuniji Miyazaki, who is currently an adviser to the bank and was president when loans to racketeer Koike began in the 1980s, would also resign, it said.
The Asahi Shimbun daily reported on Wednesday that Miyazaki told the newspaper he had had contact with a now deceased influential racketeer who had reportedly introduced Koike to DKB.
But the newspaper quoted Miyazaki as saying he recognised that the deceased racketeer had already ended his activities as a racketeer when Miyazaki had contact with him.
Japanese media reports have said DKB has supported stock investment by Koike by providing questionable loans to him.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori Koike were arrested last week on suspicion of taking some 50 million yen in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
Japan's Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.
After the Nomura payoff scandal emerged in early March, media reports said DKB had loaned three billion yen in 1989 to the younger Koike's real estate firm.
The elder Koike reportedly used the money to buy 300,000 shares in each of the nation's top four brokerages, including Nomura, and put up the shares as collateral for DKB loans.

Nomura was suspected of giving profits through securities business to the racketeer on worries about Koike's presence as a major shareholder, Japanese media reports said. The purchase of the 300,000 Nomura shares allowed Koike to make official managerial proposals at its shareholder meetings.

On Tuesday, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily said DKB had provided questionable loans worth some 600 million yen without collateral to the elder Koike in 1994. Prosecutors were particularly looking at whether the latest uncollateralised loans to Koike had violated the Commercial Code and involved breach of trust, the Yomiuri said.
